title: 300 Passes
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece uses Steve Kerr's arrival at the Golden State Warriors in 2014 as a case study in finding the single lever that changes a team's performance and culture. Kerr suspected that more ball movement would change the team's mindset, and he asked analytics staffer Sammy Gelfand to test the idea. Gelfand found the Warriors had averaged the fewest passes in the NBA, and that possessions with more than three passes led the league in scoring. Kerr made a 300-passes-per-game benchmark the cornerstone of a team-first culture, valuing it as much for the unselfish play and camaraderie it produced as for the points. The author generalizes the story into a leadership principle: great team leaders search for the "magic" action or metric that drives performance, whether it is found in data or in fundamentals everyone takes for granted. It closes by asking readers to identify their own team's 300 passes.
points: Kerr started from a cultural hypothesis, that sharing the ball changes a team's mindset, and used data to confirm and sharpen it rather than to generate it from scratch.
The decisive insight was a threshold (more than three passes per possession) that could be turned into a simple, memorable team benchmark.
The benchmark was valued less for the points it produced than for the unselfish, team-first behavior it reinforced.
The author's generalization is that difference-making levers often hide in overlooked fundamentals as well as in the numbers, and leaders must actively look for them.
quotes: His bias was to move the ball on offense with a high ratio of passes to shots. He wanted Gelfand to confirm what he suspected. Although he didn’t have any hard evidence that more passes translated to more wins, he was deeply committed to the idea that sharing the ball changes the mindset of a team.
Gelfand discovered something extraordinary in the numbers. During the previous season, the Warriors had averaged just 247 passes per game, the lowest pass count in the NBA.

When the team passed the ball more than three times per possession, they led the league in points for those possessions. Kerr pounced on this idea and made the idea the cornerstone of how he would change the culture of the team.

Even more than making baskets, Kerr believed more passing would create a team-first mindset of moving and sharing the ball, leading to unselfish play and creating the team camaraderie he believed was necessary to win championships. The Warriors won the NBA Championship that year and, under Kerr’s leadership, remain one of the best passing teams in the NBA.

Great team leaders are always on the lookout for the magic action, metric, or activity that could become a difference-maker for team performance. Sometimes, they can be found in the numbers. Other times, they can be discovered by examining the fundamental qualities of performance largely taken for granted.
